articles.title: Lamborghini Super Trofeo |Europe, Race 2: Salonen/Tuomaala take the win, Iaquinta/Gilardoni crowned champions
articles.summary: Superb recovery by the Leipert Motorsport duo, who take a 1-2 win for the team ahead of Stati/Leitch after the incident to Fraboni at the start. In PRO/AM th...
articles.body:
Matias Salonen and Henri Tuomaala claimed victory in the second encounter of the Lamborghini Super Trofeo Europe at Monza, a race that saw Kevin Gilardoni and Simone Iaquinta crowned 2026 PRO class champions.

The race was highly eventful, complicated by a persistent, intermittent drizzle that began to fall on the Monza asphalt just minutes before the start. During the formation lap, Patrik Fraboni (Oregon Team) hit the wall exiting the 'Ascari' chicane, ending his title hopes and effectively sealing the championship for Iaquinta and Gilardoni.

The first half of the race was characterised by the Safety Car. After a few laps of green-flag racing, it was deployed once again following off-track excursions by Alessio Ruffini (ASR), Philip Tang (DL Racing), and Euan Hankey (VSR). It remained on track until 22 minutes from the end, coinciding with the opening of the pit-stop window.

Following the initial lead held by Marzio Moretti ahead of Nicolas Stati, the classification shifted significantly during the round of pit stops, as teams—including those that had started on rain tyres—switched to dry-weather rubber.

The #88 Huracán driven by Tuomaala and Salonen surged into the lead; having started in sixth position, their climb through the field secured a one-two finish for Leipert Motorsport, with Stati and Leitch taking second place overall.

Rounding out the podium were Berreby and Giraud in the Villorba-entered Huracán, followed by their teammates Strignano and Pujatti, while Leitzke Grotta and Spina (Oregon Team) fought their way into the top five. Moretti and Paolo Biglieri dropped to sixth, but they were able to celebrate victory in the PRO/AM class, finishing ahead of Cristovao/Levet (VSR) and Astafjev/Cecotto (Invictus Corse), who took ninth and tenth place overall.

Positioned ahead of them were Jerzy Spinkiewicz (Uniq Racing) and the duo of Volfe/Balestriero (Leipert Motorsport).

Iaquinta and Gilardoni, who started from the back of the grid due to a fuel pump issue encountered during Qualifying 2, managed to fight their way up to 14th place, but were handed a 10-second penalty for a pit-stop infringement.

Despite a spin at the 'Roggia' chicane, Andrzej Lewandowski secured the win in the AM class behind the wheel of his ASR-entered Huracán, finishing ahead of Knoll/Kuppens (Micanek Motorsport) and Lémeret/Gillion (CMR).

In the Lamborghini Cup class, Claude-Yves Gosselin (Villorba Corse) got the better of Ostergaard/Moller Demant (DC Motorsport)—who were crowned category champions—following a hard-fought second half of the race, with Adalberto Baptista (Oregon) coming in third.

articles.title: Conte 'not in advanced negotiations' with any club amid Man Utd links
articles.summary: Antonio Conte says he is not in advanced negotiations with any club after being linked with taking over as manager of Manchester United. Reports in his nativ...
articles.body:
Antonio Conte says he is not in advanced negotiations with any club after being linked with taking over as manager of Manchester United.

Reports in his native Italy suggested former Chelsea and Tottenham boss Conte has set out conditions for his services, including over transfer policy as well as salary demands, should United decide to replace under-fire head coach Michael Carrick.

Conte guided Napoli to the Scudetto in 2025, but left the club at the end of last season after finishing runners-up to Inter.

The 57-year-old posted a statement, in both Italian and English, on his Instagram story stressing he would only consider a return to management when he believed "the conditions are right".

Conte said: "Following recent media reports in Italy and abroad, I feel it is appropriate to clarify my position.

"My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage.

"Following a wonderful and successful spell in charge of Napoli, I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management. It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right.

"I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my 'strong personality'. These reports are unfounded, as there is currently no concrete basis for such assessments.

"Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties' needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager.

"Until then, any assumptions about my demands and my professional future remain speculation and cannot be treated as fact."

articles.title: Payton Westcott Grew Up Racing. Now the Promising Teenage Driver Is Proving She Belongs In F1 (Exclusive)
articles.summary: The Laguna Beach, Calif., native tells PEOPLE about her journey from go-karting to traveling the world racing with the F1 Academy
articles.body:
Payton Westcott began competing in go-kart races at 11 after first driving a kart at age 6

The 17-year-old moved to Italy at 15 to pursue a career in open-wheel racing

Westcott earned her first F1 Academy victory in August and is targeting a top-five debut season finish

Payton Westcott has always been comfortable behind the wheel.

The F1 Academy driver grew up in a racing-obsessed household and first gripped a steering wheel on her own when she was just 6 years old, after her dad, Kevin, put her in a go-kart as a form of "babysitting."

"It was really a thing at the track we went to growing up where all the men would put their kids in karting while they would go and drive on the track themselves, and it would distract the kids for a little while," Westcott, 17, tells PEOPLE. "I drove for quite a while before one day my dad's coach noticed me and said I wasn't half bad, so he decided that he should try to put me into go-kart racing."

Westcott's family "had no idea" about the world of go-kart racing until her father's coach suggested she join — a recommendation that turned out to be a great one. Westcott continued to fall in love with racing and started competing in go-karting events at age 11. Four years later, at age 15, she moved to Italy full time to pursue racing open-wheeled cars as a career.

"I'm eternally grateful to him for putting me in racing," Westcott told F1 about her dad this past June.

Now, the Laguna Beach, Calif., native continues to master courses around the world as one of the 15 full-time drivers in the all-female F1 Academy racing series, which comes to Austin, Texas, for its penultimate event of the season this weekend. And while she does get time away from the track, Westcott tells PEOPLE driving remains top of mind as she races in a simulation at home — "whether it's going to a professional sim or just at home with my friends or playing and messing around."

An avid reader and casual television watcher, Westcott says she finds comfort in her books and cozy nights in with her family — when she has the chance to visit them back in California. But those visits have been so far between this year that her mother has lapped her in television shows they watch together. "She likes to skip ahead of me," Westcott laughs.

But there's not much time for television when there are races to be won. Westcott has continued climbing the ranks of the sport she now loves just as much as her father. Fresh off her first-ever F1 Academy win this past August, Westcott is eyeing a top-5 finish in her debut season with the racing series, designed to recruit more women into the sport's top racing series that has only seen five women enter an F1 Grand Prix weekend.

Westcott told the F1 Academy website that it was an "incredible" feeling to get her first professional win in the series. "It takes a big weight off my shoulders," the teenage up-and-comer said. "I really did it to prove to myself that I could do it, and I'm so happy."

Even as Westcott's own career blossoms, she's found inspiration from her rivals on the track.

"I definitely look a lot to the others around me," Westcott says. "I acknowledge and really pay close attention to everyone. Doriane [Pin, the F1 Academy 2025 Champion] is especially a great person to learn from."

Westcott says Pin has been coaching her this season and "it's been really helpful to have her there," pointing out the minute details she could focus on to improve her racing as her career rises. "It's really helpful to have her there giving me advice and just helping me," Westcott says. "And she's such an incredible teammate and woman. I just feel so grateful that I get to learn from her and really grow with her."

The American F1 Academy star tells PEOPLE her focus now is to "end the year on a high note."

"I'm always looking to keep improving," Westcott says, looking ahead to the series' final two events in Texas and Nevada, and then to the 2027 season. "I think in racing, the best thing is just building your career as well as building your experience and building your level. So I want to keep improving, keep moving up."

articles.title: 'Worst thing' Clemson could do in crucial stretch of 2026 is overload Tait Reynolds, OC Morris says
articles.summary: Oct. 23—CLEMSON — In crucial moments, teams rely on their best players to step up and secure victory. Clemson football is about to face a series of crucial m...
articles.body:
Oct. 23—CLEMSON — In crucial moments, teams rely on their best players to step up and secure victory.

Clemson football is about to face a series of crucial moments. The Tigers are 4-2 (2-1 ACC) in 2026, with losses to their only ranked opponents this season. Despite the up-and-down start headlined by a struggling offense ranked 109th in yards per game and 107th in points per game, Clemson will be judged by how it finishes against five ACC opponents and its annual rivalry with South Carolina.

Technically, everything the Tigers could possibly achieve is still out in front of them. But it will take a step forward from an offensive unit that has struggled, particularly in the passing game with freshman quarterback Tait Reynolds under center.

While Clemson does want more from the air offense Reynolds leads, it does not want to overstrain the rookie QB in an effort to do so, according to Tigers offensive coordinator Chad Morris. Instead, Clemson hopes to rely on the playmakers around him.

"I can't put too much on him. That's the worst thing I can do, is compound things with him," Morris said. "I got to get him in his right reads, but how do you do that? Everybody around (Reynolds) got to be better."

Reynolds took the reins of Clemson's offense late after initially losing out on the job to senior Christopher Vizzina. He got his first start on Sept. 19 against North Carolina after Vizzina fractured his elbow Sept. 12 against Georgia Southern, although coach Dabo Swinney said the change only had to do with on-field play.

Despite Reynolds having only one touchdown pass in four starts and leading the nation's 111th ranked passing offense, Swinney believes Reynolds has shown growth in his first season as a starter, and added that Clemson's latest game, a 37-0 win against Charleston Southern, was Reynolds' best.

The freshman QB passed for just 127 yards in the game, but he did go without a turnover for the first time as a starter. Swinney said drops and receivers not finishing plays, plus Clemson's choice to play backups against the Buccaneers, were more responsible for the lack of passing production than his QB's play.

"The game's slowing down for him," he said. "He's been in the fire a little bit. I think he's growing."

Just because Clemson doesn't want to overload Reynolds doesn't mean they aren't expecting him to produce. Morris said he'd like to get Reynolds more involved in the run game, but his ball security needs to improve — Reynolds has fumbled in each of his starts, but Clemson recovered the most recent instance. Swinney said winning the turnover margin, which the Tigers have yet to do this season, is the one thing Clemson must improve in the closing stretch of 2026.

"I need to do a better job with that. I keep telling everybody, 'I've never fumbled in my life.' I get out here and it's happened a couple times," Reynolds said. "It's just something to improve on and I'll fix it for sure. It's an easy fix."

Assigning more responsibility to others doesn't mean Reynolds isn't being held accountable, either. Morris said he stopped the offense in the middle of Clemson's Oct. 20 practice to deliver Reynolds a message about his pocket presence.

"The great quarterbacks that you see, when the pocket collapses, they don't look at the ground," Morris said. "They're constantly looking with their eyes down the field and seeing if they can create some explosives down the field."

Morris added that there's been flashes of it all clicking for Reynolds at once, but not enough.

While Morris and Clemson are trying to avoid adding any pressure to Reynolds' plate, it seems like the additional responsibility is only natural. Clemson will need to go through the air against a Virginia Tech defense that ranks No. 10 in the nation for least average rushing yards allowed.

It may be the "worst thing" for him, but things will likely compound for Reynolds at least a little as Clemson tries to finish 2026 strong, no matter how much Morris tries to protect him from it.

What: Clemson (4-2, 2-1 ACC) vs. Virginia Tech (5-2, 2-2 ACC)

articles.title: LPGA player poised to win $1 million Aon bonus while on maternity leave
articles.summary: Ryan O'Toole hasn't clinched the $1 million Aon prize yet but she's starting to think about how she might invest the biggest check of her career.
articles.body:
Several weeks ago, Ryann O'Toole woke up at 3:45 a.m. to the sound of her dog Louie throwing up. Worried, she decided to take him in see the emergency vet. As she was getting ready O'Toole, pregnant with her first child, started to experience stomach cramps.

The cramps came in waves and left her doubled over in pain. At the vet's office, she called her wife, who was in Germany for work, and asked her to phone a friend to come take over at the vet's office. Meanwhile, another friend met O'Toole at the emergency room as she checked in with early contractions.

O'Toole, 39, was six months pregnant at the time.

She was released after 36 hours and flew to Hawaii the next week to enjoy a vacation at the condo she'd already booked and paid for during the LPGA's Lotte Championship.

Mercifully, O'Toole hasn't had any contractions since that scare and has been cleared for light activity.

The past week, her main job was checking her phone every so often to see how Jeeno Thitikul was faring in China.

O'Toole has been on a $1 million watch since she began maternity leave following the FM Championship in late August. As the leader of the Aon Risk Reward Challenge, it made more sense to sit on her lead as golf got tougher further along in her pregnancy.

While O'Toole hasn't technically clinched the race, Jeeno Thitikul needs two double eagles in her next event, the Toto Japan Classic, to win it for a second time. (At this point, Thitikul hasn't signed up for The Annika driven by Gainbridge at Pelican, the final event before the cutoff.)

It's safe for O'Toole to start thinking about how she might invest the biggest check of her career.

"It's like winning three tournaments or a major," she gushed. "It's unbelievable."

At the start of the 2026 season, O'Toole had two main areas of focus: improve her playing status after Q-School and grow the family.

Last January, O'Toole was in Los Angeles for an egg retrieval when she got word that her brother Brennan had been in a horrific accident. She rushed back to Arizona to be by his side.

In April, she underwent an IVF embryo transfer and while playing the Mizuho Americas Open in May, she took a drugstore pregnancy test in New Jersey that came back positive. The next Monday at 7 a.m., she was outside Labcorp waiting for the doors to open to take a blood test before beginning a 36-hole U.S. Women's Open qualifier at Essex Country Club. At lunchtime, after the first 18 holes, she checked her email and confirmed the happy news.

"It took the first time, which was great," said O'Toole. "I feel very lucky."

For 15 years, O'Toole has been one of the fittest players on tour, and coming into the 2026 season, she pushed herself as hard as ever. At the start of the season, she had picked up 7 to 8 yards with driver and up to 9 yards more with 3-wood. The combination surely helped provide more opportunities for a contest that rewards strategy and risk.

"It's fun being 39, and I can still move it," she said, though she wonders what will come back post-pregnancy.

O'Toole started to focus on Aon around the JM Eagle LA Championship, where she played the designated hole in 3 under. The next week at the Chevron Championship, she finished T-7 and collected her biggest paycheck – $213,262 – since winning her first LPGA title five years ago. O'Toole made $225,000 when she won the 2021 Women's Scottish Open.

While seven-figure checks have become more common in recent years, with six coming at the majors and CME, Aon's bonus money can still be life-changing for many.

The now retired Julieta Granada became the first woman to claim a $1 million prize. The greenskeeper's daughter was 20 when she won the 2006 ADT Championship and naively thought she'd be set for life with that kind of money.

"I was young and immature, obviously," she said many years later. "You think that it's going to last forever. The reality is if I didn't win that kind of money, I probably still wouldn't be playing because it was a huge cushion to have. It is life-changing."

Carlota Ciganda won the first Aon contest back in 2019 and shed tears during the press conference as she talked about her family. O'Toole will be 33 weeks pregnant at the time of the CME and unable to travel, but there's no doubt that her smile and her story will cross the miles.

"Going into next year, I don't know when I'm going to start back up," said O'Toole. "To have this nest egg when I've got a kid coming is huge."

Beth Ann Nichols is a Golfweek senior writer covering the LPGA and women's golf .
